title: the Samkhya Karika)
hook: two travelers left behind in a forest, one who can't walk and one who can't see

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika argued that the effect is already in its cause: yogurt in the milk, oil in the sesame. What beginning did you look inside? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

A caravan has been scattered in a forest, and two travelers are left behind. One can't walk. The other can't see. Night is coming. The one who can't walk can see the path, the river, the way out, but he can't take a step. The one who can't see has strong legs and a strong back, but he has no idea which way to go. Alone, both of them stay in the forest. The classic commentaries on the Samkhya Karika tell this little story, and the Karika itself names it in a single phrase. Today it explains how the whole world got moving.
screen: `A CARAVAN SCATTERED.` → `ONE CAN'T WALK, ONE CAN'T SEE.` → `ALONE, BOTH STAY LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the ending. The traveler who can't see lifts the other onto his shoulders. Now one does the walking and the other does the seeing, and together they get out of the forest. Once they reach the village, they go their separate ways. The Karika uses this picture for the two we met when Samkhya opened. Prakriti is the one with legs: she moves, changes and unfolds, but she has no seeing of her own. Purusha is the one with eyes: the witness, who sees but never acts. Their coming together, the verse says, is like the lame and the blind, and creation unfolds from that meeting. And the Karika says what the meeting is for. It's so that purusha can see prakriti, and so that purusha can finally be set free. That's a surprise worth sitting with. In Samkhya the world isn't an accident, and it isn't a trap someone built. The whole unfolding, the gunas, the I-maker, the senses, the elements, is a journey with a purpose, and the purpose is seeing clearly. Notice too how the story ends. The two travelers part ways. That's where Samkhya is heading, and we will get there over the next two days. Not everyone in the Hindu tradition tells the end of the journey this way. Vedanta, at the close of this season, has its own account. For now, the picture is enough. A partnership that neither side could manage alone, that gets somewhere, and then lets go.
screen: `ONE CARRIES, ONE GUIDES.` · `PRAKRITI MOVES, PURUSHA SEES.` · `A MEETING WITH A PURPOSE.` · `THE TRAVELERS PART WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the two travelers sit together. Settle, and rest one hand on your knee. Very slowly, lift it a little, and lower it again. Do that a few times. The hand is the one with legs: it moves. Then notice the seeing: something is aware of the movement without lifting anything. Let the hand go still, and rest between the two. Let the body carry. Let the seeing see. If you pray, you can offer thanks for the body that carries you. The bell holds the time.
The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of the world's beginning: prakriti, who moves but can't see, and purusha, who sees but can't move, getting out of the forest together.
Your line: the Samkhya Karika. Today, notice one thing your body does for you without being asked, and let the one who notices say thanks. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Teachers of Samkhya and of Yoga philosophy explain the meeting of purusha and prakriti with the story of the lame man and the blind man, drawn from the Karika's phrase and its commentaries.

fork.setup: you're the traveler who can't see, with strong legs, lost in the forest next to someone who can't walk. what do you do?
options: set off alone and hope for the best.
lift him onto your shoulders and let him guide.
wait for the caravan to come back.
fork.reveal: one carries, one guides, and together they get out. the Karika uses it for prakriti and purusha.

original.note: Sanskrit: in Samkhya, the root of everything seen, the one that moves and unfolds.

trapdoor: what you thought: a folk tale about helping each other.
what it means: Samkhya's picture of how the seer and the seen come together so the world unfolds, with seeing and freedom as its purpose.
what a scholar hears: Samkhya Karika 21, 'like the lame and the blind', with the full story told in the classical commentaries.

notes: Karika 21 paraphrase: the union is for purusha's seeing of prakriti and for purusha's isolation (kaivalya), like the lame and the blind; creation proceeds from it. Confirm.

The caravan story (scattered by robbers in some tellings; the blind man carries the lame man; they part at the village) is from the commentaries (Gaudapada and others). Details paraphrased; confirm which commentary and the ending.
'The lame and the blind' is kept as the classic phrase; the narrative uses 'can't walk' and 'can't see'. Check the disability language is acceptable to editors.
